questions.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(1,-3,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}+y\sqrt{x}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-3,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,-3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-3) & =\frac{{1}^{2}+1}{{1}^{2}(-3)^{2}}+(-3)\sqrt{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}-3(1) \\  & =-\frac{25}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0,1,2)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)} & =(0)^{2}+(1)^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}(x-0) \\ z-2 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{\sqrt{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5 \\ z=x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3{e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|xy|$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,1) & =3{e}^{-1+1}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(-1)\cdot 1| \\  & =3\cdot 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,1) & ={f}_{x}(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\ z-(-1) & =3(x+1) \\ z+1 & =3x+3 \\ z & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,1,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3x+2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-3\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-3⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-3⟩=⟨1,0,3⟩$ is also parallel to it.

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,-6):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,-6) & =\frac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{4} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k \\  & =⟨0,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-1,1⟩.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,-1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}(2xy-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,-1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j-3\,k.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0) & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2(\frac{1}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0)(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\frac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

Example: 
                    Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,1,8)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_y = \dfrac{4x}y - 4x^2y,$ find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(2,1,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y(2,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,1) & =\frac{4(2)}{(1)}-4(2)^{2}(1) \\  & =8-16 \\  & =-8\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point

Example: 
                    Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ Given that the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x = y\cos(xy) + \cos y,$ find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,\pi)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $(1,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =\pi (-1)+(-1) \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )}(x-1) \\ z-(-1) & =(-\pi -1)(x-1) \\ z+1 & =(-\pi -1)x+\pi +1 \\ z & =-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ has the equation $y=\pi.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\pi,-1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x =  \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{4} \sin{\left(2 x + \dfrac{\pi y}{4} \right)},$ find a tangent vector to $C$ at $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0)+\frac{\pi (1)}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-1 & =\frac{\pi }{4}x \\ z & =\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(0,1,1)$ has the equation $y=1.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

To find a tangent vector, we can find a normal vector to each plane and compute their cross product.

- For the plane $y = 1,$ we write $0x + 1y + 0z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

- For the plane $z = \dfrac{\pi}{4} x +1,$ we write $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} x + 0y + 1z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = \left\langle -\dfrac{\pi}4,0,1 \right\rangle.$

Computing the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-\frac{\pi }{4},0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\pi /4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we've found a tangent vector, and this could be our final answer. However, just to make our answer a little nicer, we can multiply the vector by $4$ to yield a simpler, parallel vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)=4\,i+\pi \,k\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Just as the derivative of a function represents the slope of the tangent line to the function, the partial derivative of a function has a geometric interpretation as well.

To illustrate, consider the surface $z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$ and the plane $x=3.$ The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point $P(3,2,5)$ is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14245438/assets/8619c41cd0caf04ae9ee9bcae61e31739d8da583793a67c1c87e00186c3ac417.png)

   

To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(18-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =-2y \\ {\frac{∂f}{∂y}|}_{P} & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To verify that this result is correct, we can find the equation of the downward parabolic curve and then use single-variable calculus to compute the slope of the tangent line.

To find the equation of the downward parabolic curve, we can substitute the equation of the plane ($x=3$) into the equation of the surface ($f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$). Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,y) & =18-{3}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\  & =9-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the downward parabolic curve is $z=g(y) = 9-y^2.$ In the $yz$-plane, this curve has the following graph:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14245438/assets/e982ef5d6d8d4fec9c64957d46f22cea2a85bd002595642f58700cf48cce4256.png)

To find the slope of the tangent to $g(y)$ at $P,$ we can use single-variable calculus. We differentiate $g(y)$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(y) & =-2y \\ {g}^{′}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: The Geometric Interpretation of the Partial Derivative
tutorials.problem:
To recap, when we calculate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},$ we differentiate $f$ with respect to $y$ and treat $x$ as a constant. This is the same as finding the intersection of $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $x = x_0$ and calculating the slope of the resulting curve.

So, we have the following result:

*Suppose that a surface $z=f(x,y)$ and a plane $x = x_0$ intersect on a curve $C,$ and suppose that $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ lies on $C.$ Then $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ evaluated at $P$ gives the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$*

We have a similar result for the intersection of a surface and a plane $y=y_0\mathbin{:}$

*Suppose that a surface $z=f(x,y)$ and a plane $y = y_0$ intersect on a curve $C,$ and suppose that $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ lies on $C.$ Then $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ evaluated at $P$ gives the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$*
